extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy; authors who must formulate definitions and classifications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for composing and assessing definitions, classifying attributes (proprium/accident), and distinguishing nominal definitions from factual postulates in logical and scientific discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as declaration of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest and most correct notion of a Definition is, a proposition declaratory of the meaning of a word; namely, either the meaning which it bears in common acceptation, or that which the speaker or writer, for the particular purposes of his discourse, intends to annex to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A definition should state what a word means in use — either ordinary or context-specific. It is fundamentally a nominal proposition about language; examples and modes (direct/indirect) follow from this starting point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names are undefinable
rubrics_metrics.description: Words which have no meaning are unsusceptible of definition. Proper names, therefore, can not be defined. A proper name being a mere mark put upon an individual, and of which it is the characteristic property to be destitute of meaning, its meaning can not of course be declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to 'define' proper names by predication; one may indicate the referent (e.g., 'the son of General Thomson') but that is not a definition. Pointing or ostension, not verbal definition, identifies proper names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of connotative names by declaring connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of connotative names, the meaning is the connotation; and the definition of a connotative name, is the proposition which declares its connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can be done directly ('Man is a name connoting such and such attributes') or indirectly by predicating other connotative names that together capture the same aggregation of attributes (e.g., 'Man is a rational animal' or enumerating attributes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs indirect modes of definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct mode: state explicitly the attributes the name connotes. Indirect mode: predicate another name or names of known signification which connote the same aggregation of attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct is most precise and least equivocal but verbose and technical; indirect (using genus and/or other terms) is more usual in ordinary discourse. Choose mode appropriate to audience and required precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete (philosophical) definition = full statement of connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of a name is the sum total of all the essential propositions which can be framed with that name for their subject. All propositions the truth of which is implied in the name ... are included in the definition, if complete, and may be evolved from it without the aid of any other premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full definition analyses the complex whole into constituent attributes (analysis). For strict logical purposes prefer completeness where feasible; be aware that completeness may be impractical in ordinary use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of attributes (abstract names) via their foundation phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Every attribute is grounded on some fact or phenomenon, from which, and which alone, it derives its meaning. To obtain a definition of the attribute, we must analyze the phenomenon into these parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For single attributes, dissect the underlying phenomenon (e.g., eloquence = power of influencing feelings by speech or writing). For compound attributes, enumerate component attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of simple feelings are essentially indefinable
rubrics_metrics.description: The only names which are unsusceptible of definition, because their meaning is unsusceptible of analysis, are the names of the simple feelings themselves. These are in the same condition as proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such terms (e.g., a particular sensation) must be explained by appeal to personal experience rather than by verbal analysis; definitional work should acknowledge this limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of imperfect (popular) definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperfect or unscientific definitions take two forms: Essential but incomplete Definitions (define by part of connotation) and Accidental Definitions or Descriptions (define by attributes not part of the connotation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential-but-incomplete definitions can suffice for practical discrimination but risk being overturned by new discoveries. Accidental definitions are not genuine definitions in logic and should be treated as descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of essential-but-incomplete definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a definition states some only of the attributes connoted but those attributes are sufficient to mark out the boundary of denotation (in current knowledge), it functions practically as a definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such definitions may be used for ordinary purposes (e.g., 'Man is a rational animal'), but they are contingent on current empirical knowledge and vulnerable to counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental definitions (descriptions) are not genuine definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions in which the name of a class is defined by any of its accidents—that is, by attributes which are not included in its connotation—have been rejected from the rank of genuine Definition by all logicians, and have been termed Description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat accidental descriptions as logical definitions. They may serve to identify a class in practice but they do not explicate the term's connotation or essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convertibility/co-extensiveness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only necessary that the definition (or description) thus formed, should be convertible with the name which it professes to define; that is, should be exactly co-extensive with it, being predicable of every thing of which it is predicable, and of nothing of which it is not predicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful test of a working definition or description is convertibility: it must apply to all and only the things the term denotes. If a proposed definition is not co-extensive, it fails as a definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per genus et differentiam and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional rule that the definition of a species should be per genus et differentiam is imperfect: differentia is often taken to mean only some one peculiarity, not the whole connotation; a complete definition would include the genus and all differentiæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genus+differentia for concise definitions when appropriate, but recognize it may not capture all essential attributes; summum genus presents special difficulty for genus-based definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special/technical definitions serve classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Special or technical definition has for its object to expound the artificial classification out of which it grows; its purpose is not to expound a name's ordinary meaning but to serve as the landmark of a scientific classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting technical definitions (e.g., Cuvier's definition of man), be explicit about the classificatory purpose; they may legitimately diverge from ordinary connotation without altering denotation in that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific definitions are progressive and provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific definitions are almost always of the kind used for classification and are necessarily progressive and provisional: any extension of knowledge may lead to changes in particulars included in the science and hence in its definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and allow definitions in science to evolve (example: the changing connotation of 'acid'); avoid treating scientific definitions as final truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between definitions of names and definitions of things (postulate vs definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: All definitions are of names, and of names only; expressions commonly passing for definitions that imply the actual existence of things combine a nominal definition with a covert assertion of fact — the latter is not a definition but a postulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to separate the linguistic act (defining a term) from any factual claim about existence. When a definition-like statement implicitly assumes existence (e.g., Euclid's 'circle'), recognize that the existential claim is a postulate necessary for subsequent reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions cannot be premises for factual inference without an existential postulate
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition, being nominal, can only yield propositions about meanings of words. To reason about facts one must add the postulate that objects corresponding to the definition actually exist; otherwise one risks valid syllogisms with false empirical conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use a mere definition as the factual premise in arguments about reality (illustrated by 'dragon' example). Explicitly include any existential assumptions when relying on definitions to support empirical inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of attributes: Proprium
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proprium of the species may be defined, any attribute which belongs to all the individuals included in the species, and which, though not connoted by the specific name..., yet follows from some attribute which the name either ordinarily or specially connotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize two kinds: those that follow by demonstration (deductive inference from connoted attributes; e.g., opposite sides equal in parallelogram) and those that follow by causation (effect of a connoted attribute; e.g., understanding language follows from rationality in man). Proprium must follow necessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of attributes: Inseparable Accident
rubrics_metrics.description: Inseparable accidents are those which—although we know of no connection between them and the attributes constitutive of the species... are yet never in fact known to be absent. A concise mode: properties which are universal to the species, but not necessary to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: blackness of crows — not connoted by 'crow' as a name, but universal in known instances. Treat such attributes as current accidental universals that might be overturned by discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of attributes: Separable Accident
rubrics_metrics.description: Separable Accidents are those which are found, in point of fact, to be sometimes absent from the species; which are not only not necessary, but not even universal. They are such as do not belong to every individual of the species, or if to all, not at all times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: color of a European, being born (an attribute at one time). Attributes that vary across individuals or times belong here; they should not be used in defining the species.
